title: Does winning a US Senate seat help the party win it again? A regression-discontinuity replication of the incumbency advantage
question: In US Senate elections from 1914 to 2010, by how many percentage points does a Democratic win in one election raise the Democratic vote share in the next election for the same seat, estimated with a sharp regression-discontinuity design at a zero margin of victory?
brief: Replicate the headline sharp regression-discontinuity estimate of the US Senate incumbency advantage reported by Calonico, Cattaneo, Farrell and Titiunik (2017), 'rdrobust: Software for regression-discontinuity designs', The Stata Journal 17(2), using the data of Cattaneo, Frandsen and Titiunik (2015) distributed with the rdrobust package: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rdpackages/rdrobust/2589686d980af0eb2c0edd945d4a43e8bc081872/R/rdrobust_senate.csv (1,390 rows; outcome `vote`, the Democratic vote share in the next election for the seat; running variable `margin`, the Democratic margin of victory in the current election; cutoff 0). Use local-polynomial estimation with a data-driven bandwidth and robust bias-corrected inference. Before any outcome analysis, pre-specify the falsification checks you will report: at least a density (manipulation) test of the running variable and a test on a predetermined covariate or a placebo cutoff.

data.license: Distributed publicly with the rdrobust package for replication; no explicit licence stated for the data file

requirements: The design (polynomial order, kernel, bandwidth selector, inference method) and the falsification checks are fixed at the design gate.
Record the replicated point estimate as a result claim with id `rd-effect` (percentage points), and the robust bias-corrected 95% confidence interval as `rd-ci-low` and `rd-ci-high`.
The paper reports the published and replicated estimates side by side, with any difference explained (software versions included).
The paper says the estimate is local to close elections and does not describe it as the incumbency advantage in all elections.
